The Euphrates River. The longest river in southwestern Asia, flowing roughly twenty-seven hundred sixty kilometers from its source in eastern Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. It marks the western boundary of ancient Mesopotamia and, alongside the Tigris, sustained some of humanity's earliest and most consequential civilizations.

The Euphrates originates in the Armenian highlands of eastern Turkey and flows through Syria and Iraq before merging with the Tigris near the Persian Gulf. This river system enabled the rise of Sumer, where writing, law codes, irrigation, and urban civilization first emerged. Babylon, history's most famous ancient city, sat on the Euphrates's banks and served as the capital of Hammurabi's empire.

In recent times, dams and irrigation projects in Turkey—particularly the Atatürk Dam—have reduced the river's flow to downstream nations by half in some seasons. The Euphrates Valley was traversed by empires and trade routes for millennia and remains strategically important today. But water scarcity is becoming critical. Iraq's share of water has dropped dramatically, threatening agriculture and drinking water supplies. Archaeological sites like Uruk, Ur, and Mari line the riverbanks, preserving evidence of the world's earliest urban centers.
